::: {#rem-rarity-odds}
#### Rarity and odds

Let $x$ be an
[outcome](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-experiment-outcome)
of a [discrete random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-discrete-rv) $X$,
and let $A$ be the [event](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-event) $X = x$
with [probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-probability) $p = \P(X=x)$.
The [odds](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-odds) in favour of $A$ are $p / (1 - p)$,
and the odds against $A$ are $(1 - p) / p$ [@grinstead1997introduction, Definition 1.4].
The [rarity](#def-rarity) of $x$ is $\rarityf{x} = 1/p$,
so the odds against $A$ are $\rarityf{x} - 1$.

```{r}
#| label: rarity-odds
p_event <- c(1 / 4, 1 / 100, 1)
rarity_event <- 1 / p_event
odds_against <- (1 - p_event) / p_event
rarity_event - odds_against
rarity_event
odds_against
```

The first printed line shows that the rarity exceeds the odds against by exactly $1$ for each $p$.
An outcome with probability $1/4$ has rarity $`r rarity_event[1]`$ and odds of $`r odds_against[1]`$ to $1$ against.
The two differ by exactly $1$, so they are relatively close when the rarity is large.
At $p = 1$ the rarity is $`r rarity_event[3]`$ and the odds against are $`r odds_against[3]`$.

The odds compare an event with its
[complement](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-complement),
and the odds against take values in $[0, \infty)$ when $p$ is above $0$.
The rarity of an outcome takes values in $[1, \infty)$.
For a [continuous random variable](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-continuous-rv),
a single value has probability $0$, so it has no odds,
but its rarity is defined from the [density](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pdf).
An event such as $X \le c$ can have a probability above $0$, so it can have odds.

:::
